utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls its next witness, Mr. Van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, might I be allowed to do something that I omitted to do yesterday at the end of our working session, at the end of the examination of the witness? I omitted to tender the exhibits from the 65 ter list -- actually, one document in actual fact. The number of it is 1829, and we used that document yesterday towards the end of the day. So I'd like to tender that into evidence, with your permission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was that 1829 or 829?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be exhibit number 770, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Defence counsel's microphone please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, may you switch off your mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Aernout van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you spell your first name, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: A-e-r-n-o-u-t.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, obviously you and I both speak English. What this means for the interpreters is that, number one, we have to take our time when we speak so they can interpret what we say, and maybe even more importantly, we need to pause after question and after answer to give them time to catch up. So we both have to try to remember that. Sir, I -- I'm going to go through your background. I'm just going to read it out, unless there's an objection, and if you could confirm it. You were born on the 31st of December, 1954?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You are of Dutch and British nationality?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I'm only of Dutch nationality, but I have an English mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you were educated in England?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Largely educated in England, yes; secondary school and university.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You served in the Dutch Marine Corps, however, for two and a half years as a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You have the title of baron but you've told me that you would prefer to be called "Mr. Van Lynden."

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. After your education and your military service, you worked as a war correspondent for some 23 years?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And some of the places you worked during -- as a correspondent were in Iran, Iraq, Beirut, Afghanistan, Eastern Europe, you covered the Gulf War in 1991, you covered the conflict in the former Yugoslavia after that.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I covered those various conflicts that you mentioned. I first went to the former Yugoslavia in June, 1991, to Slovenia, and then covered most of the conflict after that until 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You worked as a war correspondent first -- you first started working for a Dutch newspaper and then you freelanced for a period of time for the Washington Post, the Observer, and BBC radio. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. That was during the late 1970s and during the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in 1988, I believe it was, you joined the staff of Sky News, which is a news service that is run out of London, I take it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In 1988 I joined Sky News, which was a new 24-hour news channel with its headquarters in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you worked there until 2001. And after that, you stopped being a war correspondent, having put in 23 years, and you began teaching, and you are now the chair of the department of journalism and mass communication at American University in Bulgaria?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now. Let's turn to the year 1991. You've already indicated that in June of 1991 you started covering the conflict in the former Yugoslavia and that you went to Slovenia and that you were then working for Sky News. Could you tell us what your assignment was when you -- when you went to Slovenia in June of 1991, what was your assignment?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: My assignment was simply to cover the events that were taking place there. On the day we arrived in Slovenia, in the evening we arrived, the Slovenes had declared independence from Yugoslavia, and a conflict then erupted between the Slovene forces, largely Territorial Defence and police, and the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long were you in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: For about two and a half weeks, maybe three weeks in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was first sent home, which at that time was in Brussels. That's where my wife was based, who is a diplomat. And after one or two days I was called by my foreign editor in London and told that they wanted me to go to Belgrade and to cover the worsening situation between Serbia and Croatia. And so I flew to Belgrade. This would have been the second half of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At that time did Sky News have any relationship, if you know, with Yugoslav television?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Right after Sky News went on-air at the beginning of 1989, the head of the international department of Yugoslav television, a man called Jaksa Scekic came to London and negotiated an agreement with the head of Sky News, whereby Yugoslav television had the rights to re-broadcast Sky News 12 hours a day, and in exchange, if Sky News came to the territory of Yugoslavia, we would be given access to pictures that had been shot by Yugoslav TV cameramen, we would be given editing facilities and other help. Originally when I arrived in Belgrade in July 1991, Jaksa Scekic came to collect me at the airport and he had organised for a local producer, who would also interpret for me as I do not speak Serbo-Croat, to go with me into the field, and the idea was that we would work with crews of Yugoslav television, Belgrade television, who were out in the field and that we could have access to those pictures but also have access to the cameramen, for instance, to shoot pieces to camera, correspondent talking directly to the camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long were you in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Only for one day, that first day and night. And then the next day, together with the field producer, Zoran Kusovac, we drove in a hired car to Bihac, which is in north-western Bosnia. We stayed there overnight, and then the next day linked up with a cameraman and a reporter of Belgrade television, in a town called Dvor Na Uni, which is just across the border from Bosnia in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would refer the Trial Chamber to page 21 of Exhibit 23, the atlas, specifically grid C3, and I think you'll find Dvor is just next to Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you went to Dvor, was it controlled by Serbs or Croats, if you could tell?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was controlled by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you arrived there, did you encounter any soldiers or fighters at the entrance of Dvor?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: One has to cross the River Una, so that's a bridge, and on the bridge or the side of the bridge there were armed Serbs who controlled us. We went with the cameraman and reporter of Belgrade television, who we had met up with in Bosanski Novi, and crossed with them. They had done this before, they were known, and therefore it was explained to the guards that we were with them, and therefore we were allowed to enter. Officially one had to have a document that one could only get in the centre of Dvor saying that one was allowed to cross the bridge. But on that occasion that was not a problem. This turned out into a Catch 22 at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll get to that. On that occasion, did you -- after you crossed the bridge there and passed through the guards, did you proceed to the headquarters in Dvor or did you go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. We were told that there had been a shooting incident overnight in a nearby village called Struga. And as I recall, we were taken or drove directly there. We drove in our own cars. On arrival there, there were -- there was a unit of the Yugoslav army that had deployed there. The man in command, as I recall, was a lieutenant-colonel in the JNA, he was a Bosnian Serb, and I met him again later on in 1992 in Brcko, in northern Bosnia. And he explained to us that his unit had been ordered into Struga really as a buffer force. Struga was a village of Croats, populated by Croats, and they had been attacked the previous evening by Serbs from Dvor. There had been shooting. We saw signs of that, bullet-holes, and what have you. No heavy use of weaponry, as far as I could see, machine-guns and other rifles. We were told a number of people had died and saw a number of people who had been killed. By the time we left, coffins were being constructed, and the population -- most of the population, had fled into the woods, and by that stage most of the population was returning to their homes after the deployment of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you remember the name of the lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember his name, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, again referring to the atlas, Struga can be found just to the north of Dvor in the atlas on page 21, in grid C3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that -- you said that some people had been killed. Do you know how many people had been killed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I recall, about four.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were these Croats or Serbs, if you know?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There are -- four Croats had been killed -- I'm sorry, let me rephrase that. I'm aware of at least four Croats having been killed. And we were told, although we did not see them at that stage, that two Serbs had also been killed. And the following day we attended the funeral of those two Serbs, and it was confirmed to us that two of the Serbs who had entered Struga, armed men had been killed in the shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just get it clear: The two Serbs who were shot in Struga had been armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were part of the force, the armed force that had entered Struga on the evening before we went there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, the -- the four Croats, did you see -- actually see their bodies?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I recall -- I'm not sure that I saw all four, but I certainly saw a couple of them, yes, and we filmed them as well. Their bodies were being cleaned prior to burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you able to see how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I recall, one of them was already partially undressed, as they were cleaning the body, as I said, prior to -- the other was not and they were dressed, as far as I could see, in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you able to tell if the -- when you saw them they were wearing the clothes that they had been wearing when they were killed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Any blood, for example, or bullet-holes or any other indication that would have suggested that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Blood, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see any weapons in connection with these bodies, that is were they holding any weapons or have any weapons on their bodies or any indication of weapons?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. There must have been some weapons amongst the villagers in Struga because at least some people fired back at the Serbs when they entered the town, killing two Serbs, but I did not personally see any weapons apart from those -- when I was in Struga apart from those of the JNA soldiers that had deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, did you learn that -- you said that Serb forces had attacked this village. Did you learn what kind of Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This was the Territorial Defence force in Dvor, and it was confirmed to us. After a few hours in Struga, we went back to Dvor and then were taken to the headquarters of the Territorial Defence forces in Dvor, and it was confirmed to us there that they had launched this attack, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you able to observe members of this Territorial Defence force, either in Dvor or in Struga?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They were no longer in Struga when we entered Struga. They were deployed on the outskirts of Dvor, in make-shift positions, barricades. Some had dug in to a degree, but these are not proper trenches, but they had taken up some defensive positions around Dvor, and we met a number of them at the headquarters. They were often only partially uniformed, so a bit of combat clothing, but not fully. And a variety of combat clothing. Some were wearing Yugoslav army clothes that they must have had from their own time, because the Yugoslav is a conscript army, they would have done military service, and the weaponry was also a mishmash of professional arms, Kalashnikovs, heavier machine-guns, but also some hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you ever able to determine where the weapons that you've described they had came from? Aside from, of course, the hunting rifles. The professional arms, Kalashnikovs, and heavier machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We asked where their armaments had been -- had come from, and we were given different answers. We were told that it was part of the normal defence for the Territorial Defence forces to have arms of this nature; others said that they had received further arms from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you described for us what you learned about what had happened, that is that these Serb forces - and you've described them as TO forces - attacked the village of Struga. Were you able to learn what the aim of the attack was?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Again, we actually got different explanations from different people we spoke to. One of the explanations, maybe this would be called the official explanation that we were given at the headquarters in Dvor, was that the aim of this operation was to rid Struga of Croatian police and -- that was the aim. Others were clearer that their aim was to rid the region of the Croats and that the aim of the operation had actually been to see to it that the population of Struga left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who, if you recall, told you that or -- I'll -- yeah. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not one of the commanders, but some of the men that we spoke to on that first day in Dvor were telling us that. For the safety of the Serbs in Dvor, it was necessary for the Croat population of Struga to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The men that you're talking about, were these -- were these Serbs, Croats?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: These were -- these were Serb members of the Territorial Defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And was -- was what they told you, that the aim of the operation was to see to it that the population of Struga left, was that consistent with what you observed when you were actually in Struga?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The population of Struga, or at least most of the population of Struga, we were told, had fled the village and gone into the hills, into the forests, when the attack took place. And while we were there, we did see people coming down from the forests, back into the village, so that seemed to confirm it. And this is also what we were told by the battalion commander of the JNA, that most of the population had fled into the forest, but they were coming back to the village. So in that sense, the operation had not succeeded because it didn't drive the people out. The people -- some of the people that we did speak to were, of course, very frightened. An attack had taken place, there had been shooting, and some of the villagers had died. And there was a clear sense of fear amongst the villagers that we spoke to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, when you say "some of the villagers had died," are you talking now in addition to the four?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is a reference to the four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, how long did you -- just kind of jumping ahead a little bit. How long did you cover the conflict in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: From 1991 until 1999. I entered Kosovo with the German forces and went into Prizren in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And so did you cover the -- all three wars; that is in Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I covered the entire conflict in 1991, the conflict in Croatia, from the Serb side -- with the Serb forces or with the JNA. I covered the entire conflict in Bosnia, but then operating on all sides until 1994 when it no longer became possible for me to operate on the Serb side. And I -- until 1994 I was in Serbia or had access to Serbia, had a visa to Serbia, and also went down to Kosovo. But in April 1994 the visa was revoked and I was called persona non grata and no longer allowed to enter Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is what you observed in Struga at the beginning of your coverage of the -- of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, is it consistent with other things that you observed during your time as a war correspondent?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, it's not consistent with what I always experienced in other parts of the world, but what -- it certainly became clear to us later in -- for instance, in 1992, in covering the conflict in Bosnia, that what we had seen there was maybe what we could call an early attempt at what the world has come to call ethnic cleansing, which happened on a large, organised scale in Eastern Bosnia during the spring and early summer of 1992. And this one incident, which was a relatively small incident in comparison to others that would follow, that we witnessed on that, I think on a Saturday morning in Struga, that this was an indication. But we didn't, of course, at that time realise that yet and I certainly would not have called it that in my report. This was an incident of fighting between Serbs and Croats. One side had attacked, both sides had suffered casualties, but I did not describe it as ethnic cleansing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. Now, after you left Struga, I think you already said you went back to Dvor. And what happened when you went back to Dvor?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We did indeed go back to Dvor. We were -- first had to go back to the headquarters --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For what reason?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We had to announce who we were and we had to be written down and get these passes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who told you to do that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This was the Belgrade journalist said that this was a necessary thing to do, that we were -- let's say, get local accreditation as a journalist. We were the first international journalists to be there. The only other journalists there was Serb journalists, so we were a novelty in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The headquarters -- can you describe what that was and who was running the headquarters, if you know.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, as I recall, there were two different buildings. There was the municipality and there was another building which was -- as I remember -- it's a while ago. It is 15 years ago that this occurred, but it was just a normal building in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who was in control -- control of this headquarters?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence forces. I believe the man who was the commander there, it was a man called Vajagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So after you went to the headquarters and got the paper, what happened?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, they wanted to talk to us and asked us questions about what we wanted to do. We explained that we simply wanted to cover the events there and see as much as possible what was happening and get an explanation as to why it was happening. These were people, you have to understand, who were not used to dealing with the international media. This was a new experience for them. So the questions were -- seemed perfectly reasonable, and we answered them. While we were there, at a certain moment, but still in the morning -- we'd begun very early in the morning, so somewhere towards the end of the morning I suppose, a -- and we were outside at the time, a black Mercedes turned up, a dusty black Mercedes, and out of this jumped a diminutive gentleman, thin, wearing a black overall, whom I recognised because I'd seen photographs of him in the international press. This is a man who became known as Captain Dragan. And he was in a state of some excitement, to say the least. Was surprised but pleased to find us there, and announced to us that he had taken -- just taken -- his forces had just taken the town of Glina and that we should accompany him there and he would show us the town that he had captured. And relatively quickly we all got into our cars -- when I say "we all," that meant also the journalist from Belgrade television, his cameraman, and three or four other local journalists. And we followed Captain Dragan in his Mercedes to the town of Glina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for your assistance, Glina can be found on page 20 of the atlas, still in grid C3. It's just north-west of Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Van Lynden, you said that he was pleased to find you there. Can you explain that; and if you know why he was pleased, tell us.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Captain Dragan had already had some attention from the international media, specifically from the British media, because while he was a Serb, he had grown up -- or at least part of his upbringing had been in Australia. He spoke good English, albeit still with an accent. And I think he felt that this was good for him to get more international attention and recognition. And I think he also felt that through people like myself his cause, as he saw it, would be given more media attention. And so he was pleased that we were there, and he was on that day very, very excited. It seemed to us that he'd had either an overdose of adrenaline or had been taking something else. I've been in war zones a long time and warfare can cause that kind of overexcitement in soldiers, but he was very hyper, indeed, on that day and he wasn't like that on other days that I met him after that. But he was clearly pleased simply for the attention that we would get him on international television.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened when you got to Glina?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We were taken straight to the police headquarters in Glina and taken into the police headquarters. There were no policemen there anymore; there were only members of Captain Dragan's militia who were all uniformed and who were clearly under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can I just pause there for a moment. Were you able to observe -- you've described his militia as being uniformed and being under his command. Can you compare Captain Dragan's militia with what you observed of the Serb TO that you described to us.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence forces were not all uniformed in the same manner, as I've already described. Some were only partially uniformed, some were in civilian clothes, some were in different sorts of combat clothes. The militia that we encountered in Glina were all uniformed in the same manner. This was a uniformed, organised militia. We later learned that Captain Dragan had been there for some time, training them in the town of Knin - that's where his headquarters were - and he showed us where he had trained his men and talked to us about training this militia. As I said, they were all uniformed in the same manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: These militia's uniforms, was it any similar to the uniforms of the TO, even though the TO's uniform was not complete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was different, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you remember the different colours of the different uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I recall, the Territorial Defence forces were partially -- if they had camouflage clothes on, they had partial -- maybe the trousers or the jacket and the shirt, or the other way around, and a variety of combat. Some were in the basic green of the JNA, some with that sort of mixture of camouflage, while the forces of Captain Dragan were all wearing the same uniform. But to be able to precisely describe that uniform to you today, I'm afraid that -- I've been in too many situations with too many uniformed men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any badges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe there was a badge. The -- it had a sort of a - how would you call it? - they had a bear, which was also -- there was an actual bear, a baby bear, at the fortress in Knin, which was the headquarters of Captain Dragan's militia. I was introduced to the bear. It was still at a baby stage at that stage. And they may have used that as a symbol. And they may also have used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who used that as a symbol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The militia of Captain Dragan. And they may also have used the colours of Serbia, but I'm not entirely certain if that was already the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I interrupted your train of thought because you were telling us about -- when I asked you about more detail about the militia that you went to a police headquarters. Was this a Croatian police headquarters or a Serb police headquarters? Could you tell at that time?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was the police headquarters in Glina, we were told. I had not been in Glina before, and it looked like a police office, certainly. There were no policemen left there, nor, as I recall, was any sign of fighting at the headquarters, or if there was it was minimal. Captain Dragan took us into the building, and he showed us what he considered to be evidence of the mentality of the people that had been in the building, the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What -- I'm just pausing. What did he show you, specifically?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Two things. On one wall a large U had been painted in the manner, as I recall, in blue paint, in the manner that U's were used during the Second World War by the Ustasha in Croatia. This is the regime that was linked to the axis during the Second World War. And the second thing that he showed us was a skull that he had found on the desk -- on one of the desks inside the police headquarters. And on this was written his name and, as I recall, a sum basically stating that Captain Dragan was wanted dead or alive for that sum of money, but I can't remember whether it was 100.000 dollars or 10.000 or a million. But he showed us -- he was holding the skull and showed it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you told us at the beginning of this account about Captain Dragan in Glina that he announced that his militia had taken Glina. Did you learn then or at any time who had held Glina before he had taken it? Who did he take it from?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He took it from the control of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you went to Glina and you went to the headquarters, what did you observe in the streets, if anything?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The streets were deserted. I don't remember seeing local population out and about at all. I didn't see any signs of any major fighting. We were not there a great deal of time. We had to follow him wherever he went, and he went first to police headquarters. And when we came out of police headquarters, another -- a different unit from the JNA than the one we had encountered earlier that day in Struga had also entered town, and an altercation then took place, which we directly witnessed, between Captain Dragan and an officer from the JNA, as I recall, a major, but I could be wrong, he could be a first captain. And with the JNA officer demanding that Captain Dragan withdraw himself and his men from Glina, and Captain Dragan telling the JNA officer that he was not planning on doing so. Having taken the town, it was now under his control and it remained so. The altercation became quite a violent one in a sense that at a certain moment Captain Dragan picked up what is known as a light anti-tank weapon. These are constructed in -- or were constructed within Yugoslavia but are also weapons that we had in NATO forces. So it was a weapon that I knew from my time in the Dutch Marine Corps. It's a weapon that's a relatively small oblong, and you pull it out, and you can fire it once and it's used against armoured vehicles, and Captain Dragan put this on his shoulder and threatened used to fire at one of the JNA tanks if the major and the JNA forces did not back down. Because of time limitations for us, at this stage we had to leave the town because we had to get our pictures and story and report back to London.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you left the protection of -- without the protection of Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left and drove back to Dvor on the same route that we had taken when we were following him there -- to Glina, but without any protection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before you left Glina, were you able to determine why the JNA was demanding that Captain Dragan withdraw himself and his men? What were they trying to accomplish? Were you able to learn that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We were not in a position to have a conversation with the JNA officer, because he was having a shouting match with Captain Dragan. We imagined that what he was doing was acting, let's say, as a buffer in the same manner that the JNA had done in Struga, but it was noticeable to us that on both occasions the JNA had only deployed after the action had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you said that you had to leave to get your story and pictures back to London. Where did you go to do that? You went to Dvor and where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We went back to Bihac. In Bihac, they have a television centre there, and we were able to edit the pictures there, and send them from Bihac to Belgrade and from Belgrade on to London.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, the next day did something happen?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The next day we went back to Dvor. I think this is the occasion that we ran into the Catch 22 situation that I referred to earlier at the bridge with the militia deployed at the bridge saying that we needed a pass to enter, but we couldn't get the pass unless we got into Dvor first. So we were left without a pass and on the bridge. Initially then we went through a rather bizarre situation of being arrested, put up against the wall, and told that we would actually be shot, that -- in the end that did not occur, obviously as I'm sitting here today. And we were allowed to enter Dvor and get the piece of paper that was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to be clear, and I'm sorry to interrupt, but the militia that you're describing, is this the same Serb TO militia that you talked about having been there the day before?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, this is the same Territorial Defence militia that I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then after that did you go to the headquarters and get the paper?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We went to -- I think it was in the municipality that we had to get this paper, but I'm not a hundred per cent certain on that, but we did get the piece of paper. We then encountered Captain Dragan again because he was giving a press conference. As I recall, he gave the press conference in -- in Serbo-Croat, but spoke to us separately, on camera, in English afterwards. We then had a conversation with him, and he told us that he was going to Knin and that we should follow him. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about what had happened in Glina?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He had told us that he had held on to the town, that the JNA had backed off.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did he say anything about Croats?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He had said the day before in the police station that the U on the wall was an indication as to why he was fighting, because he believed the Serbs population within Croatia to be under threat and because the regime then ruling in Zagreb, led by Franjo Tudjman, was of the same nature as the regime that had controlled Croatia during the Second World War. And he made the statement that what he was doing was simply protecting the Serbs and that he was adamant that the methods that he used and his militia used were those of discipline and in not hurting the civilian Croat population that they encountered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, was there -- on that day, was there a funeral either in Dvor or Struga?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There may also have been funerals in Struga, but I didn't go back there. But we went to the funeral of the two Serbs who had been killed in Struga, as I recall, in pretty dreadful weather. It was raining and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that funeral --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Was in Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was in Dvor.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was in Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, did you have occasion to go back to Dvor some several days later?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what happened on that occasion, when you went back to Dvor?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We drove into Dvor and the situation, it was immediately clear, was very tense. There were a lot of armed people running around. We had driven there. We were going to meet with Captain Dragan, and we did indeed meet up with Captain Dragan. And there we discovered he had deployed members of his militia around a building, and there was a stand-off now between his militia and the local Territorial Defence forces in Dvor that I have described before. Captain Dragan explained to us that there had been an incident in Dvor in which four or five Croat women from the village of Struga who had been getting medical attention at the medical facility or clinic in Dvor had been taken out of there by ten men of the Serb Territorial Defence forces and had been killed, hacked to pieces, according to Captain Dragan, with knives and axes. And that he had arrested these ten men and was holding them in this building which was surrounded by his militia because he felt that these men had committed a crime and should be put on trial. Again, he reiterated that he did not feel that there had to be a difference in the behaviour of the Serbs and that the Serbs should not make the mistakes of their enemies, that their enemies had made during the Second World War, a reference to the behaviour of the Ustasha forces during the Second World War, and that's why he had arrested these ten men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So if you could just kind of describe the scene for us. There is this house. The ten men who have been arrested are inside the house, and it's surrounded by Dragan's men?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Dragan's men are on the doors and around the house. A bit further away, 50, 80 metres away, there were local population, both civilian and members of the Territorial Defence forces, who wanted to get these men released. There were arguments between the commander of the local Territorial Defence forces and Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This -- is this the commander that you referred to earlier in your testimony that you thought was Vajagic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's the -- yes, it is. Dragan told a couple of his men to look after us, to keep us safe, to see that we were not attacked. And so we were not always -- I mean, we were not always constantly with Captain Dragan. We were not taken inside the house. We were not shown the ten prisoners. We were also not taken to the clinic, nor did I actually see the evidence of four or five dead Croat women. I only had Captain's -- Dragan's word to go on this. The crew and correspondent of Belgrade television were there as well but refused to film this scene of a stand-off between Serb and Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know why they refused?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, when we spoke to them and we said that this was actually what Captain Dragan was doing would probably get very good coverage by the international media as a sign that some of the Serb forces were absolutely abiding by the law. Initially the correspondent - who had been a correspondent abroad as well, he'd been in Romania during the revolution as well as I recall - agreed with us, but he said that he'd first have to call his boss. He called Belgrade television, and he told us afterwards that he had been told by his boss not to cover this, not to mention it to anyone, and to immediately leave Dvor. And he and his crew then did so. Zoran Kusovac, my producer, and I stayed behind for a time at least, but we could not film this scene because I didn't have a cameraman.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So now you've described the scene for us. The Belgrade television folks have left. Can you -- tell us what happened next.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: At a certain moment - and I cannot give he precise time - a car drew up in front of the building and out came a man, who was I was told by my producer was Milan Martic, and who -- he was described to me as sort of the commander of the Territorial Defence forces in Krajina and Banija in that region of Croatia. And there was then a meeting outside, which we witnessed, between Martic and Captain Dragan, and quite a furious argument between the two, finally ending with -- as it was translated to me by my producer, Mr. Martic ordering Captain Dragan to release the ten men whom he had arrested. And in the end that's what Captain Dragan did, when he was ordered to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you a couple questions about what you've just told us. First of all, you said you were told that this man who arrived was Milan Martic. Did you have later occasions to see Milan Martic or even meet him?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. If I recall correctly, at that stage Dragan told us to leave Dvor, told us that he was leaving Dvor and going back to Knin, and that we should follow him there the next day and that we should meet him for a late lunch, as I recall, just outside Knin. I think it's, if I remember correctly, it was The Mill or the Old Mill or something of that sort. It was an outside restaurant where there would be lamb on a -- roasted lamb. And when we got there finally, towards the late afternoon, we met up with Captain Dragan and we went there. And Milan Martic then appeared and joined us for that late lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And -- I'm just focussing on the identification here. Was it the same man that you saw in Dvor?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are now in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm now in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in Knin you had no doubt that this was, in fact, Milan Martic that you were having lunch with?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's how I was introduced to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's go back to Dvor. You said in your testimony -- you used the word, and you used it twice, that Mr. Martic ordered Captain Dragan. Did you choose that word with care? Is that what was actually translated, that he was ordering him to release the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's as I recall it, yes. That seemed to be the relationship or so. When we talked to Captain Dragan later in Knin, he described himself as not being independent but falling under the orders of Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you've described that you left and you went to Knin. And you've already told us that you've had this lunch. Can you tell us what happened at the lunch with Milan Martic and Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, it was one of those quite difficult lunches in the sense that we were speaking two different languages so there had to be translation. As I recall, Mr. Martic was sitting at the end of the table, and on one side was Captain Dragan, on the other side was myself. And I suppose that Zoran Kusovac was sitting next to me and -- to help with the translation. It was difficult in the sense that while Captain Dragan had already expressed to us in the various meetings that we'd had up to then his pleasure that international journalists were travelling to his areas -- to these areas to explain the conflict and to allow the Serbs to explain why this conflict was occurring, to make their own case, if you like. And so we also asked of course Mr. Martic for his help in doing this. But he was clearly of a different opinion. He did not seem to understand the point in journalists of my nature, international journalists, being in Knin. He didn't -- and I think I remember him actually saying this and Zoran translating that he did not really see the point in talking to someone like me, that we could not be trusted. This of course is part of the mentality that was instilled within the Yugoslav forces, certainly, Yugoslav army prior to the conflict, that nobody from the west could really be trusted that any western journalist was, by definition, a spy. And Mr. Martic's whose experience, as far as I was given to it -- to understand, was very much limited to life in a provincial city of Knin obviously felt that people of myself were either a threat or certainly could not be of any use. And the whole idea of the Serbs making a case to international opinion was a complete novelty to him and not something that he seemed to believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After you had that lunch with Milan Martic, did you have occasion to see Captain Dragan on further occasions?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. He took us to the fort overlooking Knin, as I said earlier, introduced us to his bear, with whom one had to have a sort of little struggle to prove one's manliness. And he also took us to the railway siding to show us an armoured train that he had had constructed. This was for the first time in my experience as a war correspondent that I was in a region with an armoured train. It rather reminded me of those films about the Mexican civil war in the late 19th century and early 20th century in which you saw armoured trains. I'm unaware if it was ever used. We only saw it at the railway siding of Knin. And Knin is of course above all known as a railway junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At the fortress did you observe other members of his militia, Captain Dragan's militia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We did meet other members of his militia, including some women.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know if the -- his militia was based there at the fortress or had any relationship to the fortress?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I believe that he called it his headquarters, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have any conversations with Captain Dragan about Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We spoke to him about Mr. Milosevic then, and I recall a separate conversation which was either towards the end of 1991 or at the beginning of 1992, a conversation that took place in Belgrade. He certainly saw Mr. Milosevic as being the leader of the Serbs as a whole and clearly believed that Mr. Milosevic was in charge of the entire operation, was leading the entire operation, of what was happening in Croatia at the time. When we met him in Belgrade, he asked us why it had been impossible for him to have a meeting with Mr. Milosevic. And at the time when we met him there, both Jaksa Scekic, the man I described earlier from Belgrade television, Zoran Kusovac, and myself were present, and all three of us saw this as political naivety on the part of Captain Dragan, that a man like Slobodan Milosevic would ever meet him seemed to us highly unlikely. Mr. Milosevic would keep someone like Captain Dragan at arm's length.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, going back to Knin during the times that you spent with Captain Dragan, were you able to observe anything about the funding or resources that were available to him?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There had clearly been quite some funding because all his men were uniformed in the same uniforms, as I've already described. They had modern guns, so there had clearly been funding. Precisely where this funding came from we were not told, but it's unusual for someone to immediately say: Well, we got so much from this person or from a particular government. But it was clear that he had had significant funding from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've already said that you met with Captain Dragan in Belgrade, either towards the end of 1991 or the beginning of 1992. Do you know why he had left Knin?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He told us he had left Knin because he had fallen out with Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you have -- did you talk to him about what had happened between Captain Dragan and Milan Martic in Dvor that you've testified about today?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I cannot recall talking about that in Belgrade. We did talk about it again in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did he say in Knin about it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, that he felt that this was a mistake because he felt that the Serbs should, very clearly, behave in a different manner to their opponents; in other words, that he believed that the rule of law should be upheld. And by allowing these ten men to be freed and not put on trial, he felt that Mr. Martic had made a significant mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if after you saw Captain Dragan in Belgrade towards the end of 1991 or the beginning of 1992, do you know if he ever returned to Knin?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I am told that he did, yes, but I, myself, never returned there so I did not see him myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we look at Exhibit 588 in evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we please see Exhibit 588.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It takes a moment. I think we need to have the English, though. If we could just hold it there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, this is a document which is in evidence in our trial. It's dated the 28th of July, 1991, which -- it's not evident there but it's evident on the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could just scroll down for a moment so that can be visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There, it's at the bottom. And it's from the Chief of Staff Nikola Boljanic. I'd just like you to look at point 4, which I'll just read out loud. It's quite short. "During the evening of 28 July 1991, I received information of an uncontrolled and notorious deed by the members of the sabotage platoon, who that day killed patients (women) at the Medical Centre in Dvor." Is that consistent with what you heard had happened when you went to Dvor on that day?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was not told that they were members of the sabotage platoon; at least I don't remember being told that. What captain -- what I remember Captain Dragan telling us was that these were members of the Territorial Defence forces, but that's what he said had happened. And he mentioned four or five women. And as I said, as I recall, he said that they were actually from Struga but that they were at the medical centre or clinic in Dvor when they were taken out and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When is the first time that you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: You showed it to me on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was this after you had given a -- already given a statement about this event?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I gave a statement about this event several years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- we're just a couple of minutes before the break, but the next topic will take longer. So perhaps if we could just take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask one or two questions now just to take us to the last -- to break time. After the lunch in Knin, did you ever see Mr. Martic thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour. I saw him in what would have been probably late February 1994 when he visited Pale in Bosnia, and he was visiting officially as the president of the Serb republic in Croatia, I don't know the precise name it gave, and he was visiting his counterpart, Dr. Karadzic, who was the president of the Bosnian Serbs, at his headquarters in Pale. This was after the first market explosion in Sarajevo, and I was then based in Pale. It was snowing, as I recall. Mr. Martic reviewed a military guard of honour and then went inside the building known as the Bosnian Serb Presidency for talks with Dr. Karadzic. But I was there and I saw him then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you came to know him fairly well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't have -- when I saw him then, I didn't have a conversation with him. So my only face-to-face conversation with him was during that late lunch just outside of Knin in July 1991. That's the only conversation I personally had with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you know him facially?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can identify him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I ask for now. Court adjourned. We'll come back at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, I'm going to show you a clip, a video clip, on the monitor that's -- that's in evidence. It's in evidence as Exhibit 479. We don't need to call it up because we can show it from the Sanction here, but I think we have to switch over to the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're going to have to tell us how to switch over to the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, you don't need to do anything. I think it's been taken care of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: We'll have to be reminded of what the Sanction is, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Sanction is a computer programme that we have here that allows us to show videotapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is -- at the beginning where you see TV Belgrade, do you recognise this image?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. As far as I can see, this is a shot of Knin taken from the fort.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this image?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The man in the uniform is Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If the record could reflect that the witness has identified Milan Martic in the video clip, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. While the video clip is there, can I just ask a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That uniform that Mr. Martic is wearing, how does it compare to any of the uniforms that were worn by any of the people that you saw on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall him wearing that uniform when I met him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, I understand. But this one that he's wearing now on the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How does it compare with any of the uniforms that you saw in Dvor? Does it resemble any of those that you saw there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of the men may have been wearing this, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not able to say which men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's 15 years ago, and I've seen a lot of war in the meantime. I can't remember every uniform that every soldier has worn, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, just following on what Judge Moloto asked, what about the badges, the insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The insignia changed over time, and I would have to put on my spectacles. They may have already had those insignia in July 1991, but I cannot recall precisely and, therefore, I think it's probably better for me to say I don't know to be -- in all honesty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And we'll just continue with the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we pause it here, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, do you recognise anybody in this image?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The man wearing the beret is Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Being interviewed, the man being interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that probably sufficiently identifies it, but just -- in case there's need, I'll put on the record the time stamp which is 00:31:15.3. And he's the only man wearing the beret in the image and he's being interviewed. Thank you. I'm done with that exhibit. And in fact, those are all my questions. Thank you very much, Mr. Van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the cross-examination of this witness will be conducted by my colleague, Mr. Nikola Perovic, co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Van Lynden, I assume you've understood that I'm one of the counsel, co-counsel, of the accused, Mr. Milan Martic, and I'm going to start the cross-examination, as provided for by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in this Tribunal. From your personal data, your CV, I see that as a correspondent you worked for 22 years as a war correspondent, in fact?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You also state that you were a reserve officer, a lieutenant, in the Netherlands navy?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I was a second lieutenant [Realtime transcript read in error "lieutenant-colonel"] in the Royal Netherlands Marine Corps, not in the navy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And today I heard in response to a question from the Prosecutor, that you have completed secondary school. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just point out that it's written here that I was a lieutenant-colonel. I wasn't a lieutenant-colonel, I was merely a second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see what's written there says: "No, I was a 2nd Lieutenant-Colonel" -- oh, yes, second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, to come back to your question. Yes, I completed secondary school in the United Kingdom, and then also I did a bachelor degree at university in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In what course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In sociology, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank the Court for its assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I have just asked you that because in your CV that portion was lacking, at least the CV and the information that I had before me. On two occasions you made statements for the Prosecution, once in 2001 and the second time in 2002. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So you confirm that you gave those two statements. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I gave two statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And both are within the e-court system, so if necessary, we'll be able to refer to them in due course. In September 2003, you also testified before this Tribunal at the Slobodan Milosevic trial. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: September or October 2003, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You started reporting from Croatia in July 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, as I've already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was that the first time you visited Croatia, after the crisis started?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So before that you didn't have any direct knowledge about the events in those parts?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I had been in Slovenia in June and then the first part of July 1991. I did actually visit Zagreb on one day, but that was simply to send a story from the Slovene-Croatia border because Zagreb television was closer than Ljubljana television, but I didn't spend any real time in Croatia. So this is my first time in the zone of battle, if you like, within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So that was the first time you gained first-hand knowledge about the events in Croatia, in July 1991. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That would be right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: However, when you started reporting from Croatia, as far as I understood it from your statement, you weren't permanently stationed over there but your headquarters were in Bihac, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We stayed in a hotel in Bihac and used the facilities of the television stations in Bihac, but the work during the day took us into Banija and later into Krajina. But really where I was based was Belgrade, and that's the base that I would keep throughout the rest of 1991, sometimes taking me to Vukovar, sometimes taking me to Cavtat and Dubrovnik areas. It depends on where the fighting was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: At the time there was no conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, right, when you were in Bihac?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There was no conflict in Bihac in 1991, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to understand from your statements, you sent your reports via satellite communication, satellite link from Bihac. Is that right? Would that be the right conclusion?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I recall, it went from Bihac to Sarajevo, from Sarajevo to Belgrade. In Belgrade the report would be taped and separately sent by satellite from Belgrade to London. Precisely the link between Bihac and Sarajevo, I'm not aware of the precise link that this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you didn't have the possibility of doing that from the area from which you were reporting?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, there was no link to do it from Dvor, for instance. One could do it from Knin, but not from Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So each time you sent out your report, you had to go to Bihac. Right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said something about that today, and also this is contained in your statements. You said that as soon as you arrived in Bihac, that first morning, you crossed the border on the River Una and reached the village of Struga. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We had arrived in Bihac the previous evening, and on -- what I recall, but I may be wrong, was a Saturday -- early on the Saturday morning we met up with the correspondent and cameraman of Belgrade TV in Bosanski Novi and then crossed over the bridge into Dvor and drove on with them to the village of Struga.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When you reached Struga, as I understand it from what you said, the units of the Yugoslav People's Army of the day were already deployed there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And I further conclude from that that the conflict that you talked about had already finished, was already over. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You also said in your witness statement that it seemed to you that the commander of those JNA units really did try to separate the two sides involved in the conflict. Is that what you said, the two groups?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was our impression, that he had been ordered to deploy to see that there was no further fighting, and that he was sincere in doing that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In your second statement in 2002 to the Prosecution you talk about this group on the Serb side as being a Serb militia, and you explain that when you say "Serb militia" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there have been now several questions about the statements of the witness. I wonder if they could be made available to him if there are going to be questions. I also -- I suggest that they would be made available to him in hard copy. I think it's very hard to follow on the e-court the statements and follow along where they are, especially when it jumps around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, do you have hard copy statements in English for the witness, hopefully also for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I thought the statements were in the system; that's why I haven't got them in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. Mr. Whiting, it doesn't look like we've got hard copies, and I think it was quite legitimate to -- not to provide hard copies if he thought that they can be found in the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I have no objection to everybody using hard copies -- the e-court system. I do think that for the witness, if there is a hard copy, it's -- I think it's easier. I just -- with the last witness it tended to get off the screen and then back on, and it just -- I didn't think it worked very well. So if there's one hard copy for the witness and everyone else can follow on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand, but I don't think -- I think what Mr. Perovic is saying is that there isn't such a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have one copy in English. It is the February 2002 statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. And you don't have a copy of the other statement, the second statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have a copy of the other one that's unmarked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, thank you very much. And then can we have it on the system so that -- for those of us who don't have the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Can we have these statements on the system, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I resume, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may resume, Mr. Perovic. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Van Lynden, you now have both statements in front of you so you'll be able to use both of them. We were talking about the 2002 statement and page 2 of that statement. You called the group on the Serb side, as you referred to it, as the Serb militia. And you explain that: "By Serb militia, I mean local armed Serbs, not the regular army." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, otherwise you can call them the Territorial Defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I wanted to ask you. Today for the first time you used the term "Territorial Defence." You didn't do that on the first or the second occasion when you gave your statement, neither did you use that term during your testimony in the Milosevic trial. So you're mentioning the Territorial Defence for the first time today. Previously you've referred to these men as the Serb militia. Do you equate the two? Is it the same?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: For instance, with Captain Dragan, I would call that a separate militia. With these men and those that I encountered in other places, it was. But it's not always the same, no. But, as I recall, the men that I saw in Dvor came under a command that was part of the Territorial Defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You described to us what the members of these units looked like. You said they were people who wore different types of uniform. Some of them were in camouflage uniform, mixed with civilian clothes, others had hunting rifles, others again had Kalashnikovs or machine-guns. Is that the description you would give us today as well?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's the description I have given today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So they weren't members of the police force?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. The police force would have worn a different uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You also said that in the conflict in the village of Struga, among others, two Serbs were killed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's correct. I went to their funeral on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity of seeing one of the members of the group that took part in the conflict on the Croatian side, so a Croatian member?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I have no recall of meeting any armed Croat while I was in Struga. I saw, I think, two of the dead and they didn't appear to me to have been members of the police. They were certainly not in police uniforms, and whether these men had been carrying weapons or not, it was impossible for me to tell. They were male.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: However, from the fact that these two Serbs were killed, I conclude that the Croats would have had to have been armed as well. Would you agree with my conclusion?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Absolutely. And as I've already said to the Court in my earlier testimony, there must have been men with guns who fired back when they were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you exclude the possibility of those armed Croats who opened fire when they were attacked were, at the same time, members of some organised military unit, for instance, regardless of the fact that they were wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was not told, also not by the lieutenant-colonel of the JNA of the presence of any armed military unit. We asked, but he said that he was not aware of any such Croat military unit being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: After that you went to Dvor Na Uni, where you met Captain Dragan for the first time and he took you to Glina; and, as you told us, his forces had just taken control of Glina, as he explained to you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In that same statement of 2002, on page 2 again, you described Captain Dragan's men, and you said that they had their own uniforms, not western camouflage and not the JNA ones either. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's as I remember it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Would you now be able to tell us what those uniforms looked like that Captain Dragan's men wore? Would you be able to describe them better or more closely now? If you can't remember, I don't insist.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. As I have already said to the Judges, I don't have a precise recollection of these uniforms, no. I do have a recollection of them being different and recognisably different, but precisely why -- I'm sorry, I've seen too many uniforms in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. On page 3 of that same statement you say that Captain Dragan took you to the police station in Glina where he showed you a human skull, on which it said "Dragan" and that there was a text on the skull reading: "Wanted dead or alive." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Words of that nature. But as I recall, written in Serbo-Croat and not in English. So this was translated for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In that same statement - and you said something about that today as well - that on the walls of that police station the letter U had been written up. Can you explain what that letter means or those letters mean?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Again, as I've already said in earlier testimony, this U was painted in the manner that I was told had been used during the Second World War during the regime of Ante Pavelic, the Ustasha regime, so this stood for "Ustasha."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croatian forces have control of that police station previously; do you know that? I mean the police station in Glina to which Captain Dragan took you. Was it in the hands of the Croatian forces before that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was, I imagine, controlled by the Croatian police. It was a police station -- so yes, but by the Croatian police, not by any other kind of force that I am aware of, nor did Captain Dragan say anything else that anybody else had been in it, just the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The following day, you saw Captain Dragan once again at Dvor Na Uni at the burial of the Serbs who were killed in Struga. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
