utterances.text: No, I did not see him at the funeral. He -- I saw him earlier in the day when he gave a press conference. I don't remember him attending the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When he spoke about the fact that all the Croats under Serb control should be treated in the proper manner, properly, and that the Serbs should not make the mistakes that his enemies had made -- that their enemies had made - you remember speaking about that - did Captain Dragan leave a sincere impression on you? Did he -- did you think he was sincere in what he was saying?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was our impression, that he meant this, that he was aware that it would seriously affect the standing of Serbia and the Serbs in the international community if they were to make the same mistakes that the Ustasha had made in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said something about the people that Captain Dragan commanded. You also said something about that at the Milosevic trial, and you said that those people seemed to be more disciplined and better dressed and equipped than other members of armed formations. Was that your impression?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Compared to the men that I had seen in Dvor, yes, this was a -- looked like an organised unit. There was discipline. There was a hierarchy of order, of commanders, and it appeared to us - and when we asked him he confirmed it - that these men had been trained for a period of time. He did not tell us for how long they had been trained, but he said that they had undertaken training, and that's why it was an organised force that he was -- and disciplined force that he was leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said something today about the captain or altercation between Captain Dragan and a high-ranking Yugoslav officer in Glina, but when asked by the Prosecutor you couldn't tell us any more about that, why the altercation took place in the first place, what the clash was about.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No -- I think I did, actually, explain that this -- as I recall, the major, but I may be wrong in the rank of the Yugoslav officer, but that he ordered Captain Dragan and his men to leave Glina and that was the reason for the altercation. And I think that I did mention that in my earlier testimony to the Court. Captain Dragan refused to leave, and therefore there was this altercation between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. Maybe my question wasn't as precise as it should have been. What I wanted to ask you was this: Were you able to discern why this JNA officer asked Captain Dragan to leave Glina or, rather, to leave it to the Yugoslav People's Army, as the regular units. Were you able to deduce that from anything they said?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I think I've also explained to the Court, I was not in a position to actually have a conversation with this officer because he was in the shouting match with Captain Dragan. But we imagined, and he may well have said that he had orders from higher up within the Yugoslav People's Army, to see to it that Captain Dragan withdrew his militia. And therefore, I imagine this officer was simply trying to carry out his orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What language did they speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They spoke in what I would call Serbo-Croat, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You wouldn't have understood what they were saying to each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but I had my producer with me, who was translating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, when you said he may have said that these were orders from above, is that an assumption on your part or is that what your co-producer told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no absolutely precise recollection of that one conversation 15 years ago, Your Honour, but I do remember that he clearly said that Captain Dragan should leave and his men should leave Glina and that the JNA should be allowed to take over control. The precise manner of words, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you don't know whether that's an assumption on your part or something you heard from somebody else? You said he said to you -- you said: But we imagined he may have well have -- he may well have said that he had orders from higher up within the Yugoslav People's Army --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I cannot precisely recall whether he said he had orders or not, but he -- what I do recall is that he told Captain Dragan and his men to leave. Whether -- I imagine that that's on a basis of orders from higher up, but that I don't know for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You imagine. Thank you. Sorry, Mr. Perovic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: A few days after the funeral, were you -- or rather, you were not in Dvor Na Uni anymore?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I recall, we had a -- whether it was precisely the day after or a couple of days, that I don't precisely remember when we met up with Captain Dragan in Dvor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you met again in Dvor, you met Captain Dragan there, and he told you on that occasion that he had arrested some local Serbs - you mentioned about ten of them - for whom he claimed they killed four Croatian women. Is that correct? You were told this by Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We were told this by Captain Dragan. I never saw the women myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the only thing you know about the event is what you were told by Captain Dragan himself?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell you what unit those ten men belonged to, the ten that he had detained?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: From the -- the local forces in Dvor, local Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Is that your conclusion or was -- were you told this by Dragan?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's what I remember him telling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did Captain Dragan at the time explain to you how he came to learn about that murder and did he explain how he managed to establish that those men he had detained were the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't remember him giving a precise explanation as to how he had found out. We imagined that he had been in Dvor and he had heard about it, but we don't know from whom. And I don't remember him telling us in detail about how he had learnt about this, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On page 3 of your statement from 2002 you mention how impressed you were with Captain Dragan's resolve to punish the men for whom he held -- thought were responsible for the murders. You said you were impressed by his resolve in that regard. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was impressed with his resolve to see to it that the rule of law remained in place. I mean, he wasn't -- he felt that these people should be on -- put on trial for the acts that they had committed; that's the rule of law. He wasn't taking the law into his own hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you've provided an answer which now forces me to ask the following question: Did Captain Dragan have any such authority to arrest and institute proceedings against people who may have committed crimes, since we are discussing the rule of law?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't think he would claim to have had the power to institute proceedings, as you put it. He felt that he did have the authority to arrest the men. Whether he actually had that authority was not up to me. I mean, I just witnessed that he had arrested these men. Whether that was part of the rule of law, you would have to ask other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: But you don't know that as -- for a fact, do you, whether that was within the rule of law, the conduct of Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He was not the police and he had arrested ten men. In a usual state, it would be the police who would arrest such people. The circumstances, of course, were not normal ones. There was already a conflict, and that, I think, is why he believed that he had the authority to act. Whether that is within your definition of the rule of law or not, that's the way that the situation was on the ground, that he felt that he did have the power and the authority to act at that time. But not ever did he say to us that he would put these people on trial; he would hand them over for trial. To whom, it was unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: As regards this incident, you mentioned that a man arrived subsequently and that you were told that that was Martic. You mentioned the argument Captain Dragan had with him, which was concluded by Martic ordering Dragan to release those men. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is -- that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The argument between the two of them took place in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we now return to the problem mentioned by Judge Moloto. You couldn't have understood the exchange, could you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, but I had Zoran Kusovac with me translating. And Captain Dragan came to us afterwards to tell us that he had been ordered to release the ten men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So you were told by Captain Dragan. You said that Captain Dragan was quite upset and angry because he was forced to act in that way. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, he felt that this was a mistake because he felt that, as I have stated earlier, that the Serbs should not make the same errors as their enemies and that if a crime was committed by any Serb, that is Serbs should be tried for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, he cared to see that through, to have those who committed a crime tried?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's what he told us that he wanted, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Then you spoke about the next day. You said that you were in Knin at a lunch with Captain Dragan and Milan Martic. On that occasion, did you notice an animosity, a tension between the two? I'm asking you this because it seemed logical for that to occur, having in mind their argument the day before.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't notice a particular animosity or tension. Captain Dragan told us that he was -- felt that a mistake had been made, but he had had to follow the orders of Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Today you were shown a document, that being a letter by Nikola Boljanic, who was chief of the war staff at Dvor Na Uni, at least that is what is stated in the document. During the relevant time, did you know of the existence of such a war staff and the aforementioned person in Dvor Na Uni?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was aware that there was a certain chain of command there. Whether they called themselves a war star staff, no, I wasn't -- I don't recall being told that. I may have met this man. I don't remember his name. The only name I remember from Dvor is, as I recall, someone called Vajagic, who I think was the commanding officer there of this Territorial Defence, or the militia, whatever you wish to call it. That's the only name that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You were shown the document by the Prosecutor, and you had an opportunity to read it. Apart from the event in the village of Struga, if we leave that aside, did anything else in the document ring a bell, apart from that event? That was in paragraph 4 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I think it would be fair to show the document again to the witness, if he is going to ask that sort of a question about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was going to suggest to Mr. Perovic. You can tell him exactly what it is you want to talk about, Mr. Perovic, you remember? You're cross-examining. Just tell him, and if -- you can also refer him to the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For assistance, it's Exhibit 588.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 588. We had it on the screen a minute ago. That's the report by Nikola Boljanic, chief of war staff at Dvor Na Uni.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We may have that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please scroll down to reach paragraph 4. That is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 mentions the event of the 28th of July, 1991. It states: "During the evening ... I received information of an uncontrolled and notorious deed by the members of the sabotage platoon, who that day killed patients (women) at the Medical Centre in Dvor." That is the event I referred to. You were told this by Captain Dragan, and that was the event because of which he arrested the men we mentioned previously. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I imagine to be correct, yes. Although I don't have a recall of the precise date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I cited the date from the report. Of course I understand that you may not be able to remember the exact date. Apart from that event and concerning the other events from the document, they are unfamiliar to you. You have no knowledge of those, do you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Can I just read through the entire document in that case? Is it possible to just go to the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Okay. No, I'm not aware of those other events.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, these other events are unfamiliar to you. As regards the event in Dvor, you can see in the report that Boljanic states that members of a certain sabotage detachment, as according to the information he had, perpetrated that crime, members of the sabotage platoon. Did you know about that before this report was shown to you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't remember Captain Dragan ever telling us that it was members from a precise unit, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood your answers during the testimony in chief and having read your previous statements given to the OTP, I conclude that you had only one direct contact or meeting, and that was during the lunch in the environs of Knin. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: One meeting with Milan Martic is what you are asking? Yes, that's the only face-to-face and that we talked to each other, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You described Martic as the kind of person who wouldn't be interested in journalists. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I described him as not seeing any value in spending time with international, foreign journalists; whether he was willing to spend time with local journalists, I don't know. But with people like myself, foreign correspondents, he did not seem to be interested in talking to us, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In that context, in one of the answers provided during your testimony in chief, you stated that you were under the impression that, by definition, all journalists were spies to him, which was typical of the old Yugoslav communist mentality. Hence, my question: What is this typical old Yugoslav communist mentality?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can I just -- I'm sorry, but I hate to be precise here but I think it's important. I think that question slightly misstates the evidence, because as the witness has just explained what he's talking about was foreign journalists, and the last question doesn't make that clear. It again talks about all journalists. If that could be made clear, then otherwise I don't object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought it was rather clear that we were talking about foreign journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Based on your description of Martic's mentality, one concludes that he did not believe foreigners, and that as far as he was concerned all foreign journalists were spies, which was typical of the old Yugoslav communist mentality. Is that correct? That was in the first statement given to the OTP. I believe you have that before you on page 16.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That was indeed my impression. That was also confirmed in later dealings with the Yugoslav People's Army, specifically around Vukovar, where we met officers who, simply by definition, because we were foreign journalists felt that we -- that they were, therefore, untrustworthy and probably spies. And it was my impression at the time that Mr. Martic, who came out of the police, was of a similar mentality and did not understand or have the same understanding as Captain Dragan did that our presence was actually an opportunity for the local Serbs to make their own case to the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And this is what you understood as the old Yugoslav communist mentality?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was also explained to me by my producer that within the armed forces or within the police forces there was an engrained, in-built distrust of foreign correspondents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: As regards Martic, you also said this on the same page, the same paragraph, that he was a provincial person who knew little of Yugoslavia beyond the boundaries of Krajina and let alone about Europe. Your conclusion was that he was a small-time provincial cop. Were those your words? Paragraph 5, page 16, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Paragraph 5, page -- I don't have five paragraphs on page 16. You may have the Serb translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that's where the misunderstanding is because I'm looking at the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Ah, yes, I have found what you -- it's actually on page 18 in the English translation. That was my impression of Mr. Martic, that he was quite different in his mentality with dealing with figures like myself than, for instance, Captain Dragan, who had been elsewhere. And that -- yes, that's -- I would stand by that. That was my impression at the time following this one lunch conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This impression of yours is what you mentioned in your statement to the OTP by stating that he was a provincial type of person and a small-time provincial cop. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's what I've written in the statement -- that's what's written in the statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Would you deem that to be an insult, such a way of thinking about someone?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. I was asked for my impression and gave my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What would you say if someone were to say that you were a nosey parker from the wide world? Would that be an insult?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object. I think that's -- that's argumentative and it's really irrelevant and it's not treating the witness properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I clarify, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Respond to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course it is unfounded, but -- and argumentative, but I compared two possible insults. One stated by the witness as regards the accused, and I just wanted to put him in a hypothetical situation, if he were characterised in a similar way, to see whether he would object to that. That's why I don't agree with the objection in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is objectionable, for starters, is that you are being argumentative. The witness has explained to you that he was asked for his impression, and he gave his impression. And if you find that his impression was offensive, then he probably didn't have any other way of putting it other than -- if he was to say honestly what he thought, that's what he thought. And what we want to know now today is just the facts of the case, not what he would think or how he would feel if he was addressed similarly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness's impression of the accused is not what I find insulting, but rather the words he used. Since he finds no insult in stating that someone is a provincial person and a small-time provincial cop, I just asked the witness whether he would be insulted if someone were to say something similar in a similar situation for or about him. I didn't want to go beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is disallowed, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In your statements given to the OTP and during your testimony today -- or from your testimony, I would conclude that you think highly of yourself. You were a war correspondent for a great number of years and you claim for yourself to be not in the least biased?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object. The -- certainly to the first part, which I don't think is relevant. And with respect to the second part, the bias, I think that's vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 16 in the last paragraph, I don't know where that is in the English version, in B/C/S it's page 16, the last sentence -- I think it's on page 18 of the English. The witness says of himself that: "I wasn't at all biased," and I was quoting him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is your response to the first part, "you think highly of yourself"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, you said -- when Mr. Whiting objected, you had said the following: "In your statements given to the OTP and during your testimony today -- or from your testimony, I would conclude that you think highly of yourself. A war correspondent for a great number of years and you claim for yourself to be not in the least biased." Now, Mr. Whiting has objected to the statement that you say the witness thinks highly of himself and also to the statement that you say he doesn't -- he thinks he is not in the least biased. You have explained to us why you use the word "biased" because he has used it himself in his statement. My question to you is: What is your response to the objection to the first part of that statement by you; namely, that the witness thinks highly of himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Highly of himself or has a good opinion of himself, that doesn't matter, it's the same thing. But if someone says he's a very well experienced professional of a war -- being a war correspondent for many years, that he's completely objective and non-biased, then I conclude that he has a good opinion of himself, and that's why I ask that, because they are the words the witness used to describe himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure -- are you saying that in the statement the witness said he thinks highly of himself? If you say those are the words he used to describe himself? He just told what his experience is as a war correspondent, but does the fact that one gives one's curriculum vitae mean that that person thinks highly of himself or are you just explaining who you are?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that, Your Honour, and I will re-formulate the question and leave out anything that creates a misunderstanding. So the witness has said that he's an experienced journalist, a true professional, and that he wasn't in the least biased. Those are his words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Now, my question is this: Whether he is certain and quite convinced that he wasn't perhaps biased in reporting from the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that I was biased in reporting from the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And just one more point. You state in the summary, the penultimate sentence says: "The world could see where the blame -- the greatest blame lies." And in that regard I have the following question: What do you mean by "the world," when you say "the world"? Do you mean your great news agency network or what? What do you consider to be "the world"? When you say "the world was able to see where the greatest blame lies," what did you mean by "the world"? I'm asking you that because this Court in this case and other cases is here to establish where the blame lies, who is to blame and to what extent. Now, 15 years ago you say that "the world could see where the greatest blame lies." So what do you mean when you say "the world"?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I didn't say 15 years ago; this is written in the statement. I believe that the reporting that was done by journalists, not just by myself but by hundreds of journalists, of the events that occurred during the 1990s in the former Yugoslavia showed, quite clearly, to anyone who was watching, reading, and listening what occurred during that conflict and where the majority of the fault lies. As far as I am aware, the work of this Tribunal is to try individual members of the -- citizens of the former Yugoslavia for individual crimes they committed. Those are two separate things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So can you give me an answer? What is "the world" as far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I meant the outside -- the international community, anyone who reads newspapers, watches television, or listens to radio. I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And that's your answer?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that completes my cross-examination. I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Whiting. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, please. Just a clarification about this understanding of the role of a journalist in such times. You spoke about the "in-built distrust to foreign journalists" in certain situations. And this you wouldn't regard a phenomenon of former Yugoslavia only, would you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Certainly not, Your Honour. I've encountered this in countries like Iraq, Iran, and indeed I live in a former communist state, Bulgaria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: More of a general nature?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It's more of a general nature, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No questions from this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I also have no questions. I think mine were answered during your testimony. Thank you very much -- I beg your pardon. Any questions arising from Judge Hoepfel's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Van Lynden, thank you so much for coming to testify. The Bench -- the Chamber is quite grateful to you for your time. This brings us to the end of your testimony. You are excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want to call your next witness or shall that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, actually, Your Honour, we do not have another witness for today. We had expected -- we had expected that Mr. Kirudja would finish today and then when we made the arrangements to sit longer, we had already sent our next witness home, and so we don't have another witness until Tuesday. I do have two small housekeeping matters to take care of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The first is I would just ask if -- I think it was clear towards the end of the cross-examination there that -- with this last witness that Mr. -- that Defence counsel was making references to the statement of the witness and the witness had the statement but nobody else did and it wasn't come up on e-court. It seems to me that it's not an efficient practice to have the statements up an e-court because documents get up and then the statement comes down. And so if we're going to -- I would ask that we adopt a practice that if there's going to be cross-examination on statements that hard copies be provided. I think that that works better. Secondly, the Court on -- ordered us to make selections with respect to those exhibits, and we have done so, as ordered, with respect to Exhibit 24 and Exhibit 476. Our selection has been loaded up as a separate exhibit into e-court. I can give the document ID numbers, and if the registrar could be asked to assign exhibit numbers to -- I don't think there is a need to call it up, but if we could just assign exhibit numbers. With respect to the Exhibit 24, our selection is under document ID number 0035-9426.1; and with respect to Exhibit 476 the -- our selection is under document ID number in e-court 0115-7663.1. So I think all that needs to be done is if the registrar could be asked to assign exhibit numbers to those two documents, those two batches, as it were. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic -- I beg your pardon, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: If you didn't want to react to that. Wouldn't that remain the same exhibit numbers and the old material taken out?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's one way to do it, though if the Defence makes -- also makes selections, then that's going to have to be a new -- theirs will have to be a new exhibit. But it's -- however -- whatever's most convenient and works best. The old exhibits could be taken out ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And am I right to say that it is not possible in the -- we are coming to you, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm not -- I'm not disregarding you. Am I right in saying that in the e-court it's not possible to have an A and B section of the same exhibit? You can't say Prosecution's exhibits, for instance, are 24A; and those from the Defence would be 24B? That's not possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence will accept the standpoint of the Court, which indicates the most rational way to proceed. Of course, that is food for thought, and I'm sure that there -- there will always be a problem if we have duplication. But with your permission I would like to say one more thing with respect to the books. When the Trial Chamber asked me to give my opinion of one book or provide a copy of one book, I later realised that it was all three books that were concerned. So I should like to ask the Trial Chamber to extend the deadline because I had to adjust our work schedule for just one book. Why I understood it to be just one book that you were requiring, I don't know, so please accept my apologies, and I'd like to have until next Monday for all three books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There were three exhibits, Mr. Milovancevic. Each exhibit related to a book. How you could have thought that it was one book I do not understand. However, we are not even sitting on Monday; it will have to be Tuesday. Can you make sure that you let us have those on Tuesday? Can I come back to my question: Is that possible to have an A and a B?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just finish, Mr. Milovancevic? I'm going to suggest then that registry finds the best way to give exhibit numbers to those documents, the best way you find. What I think is of interest to the Chamber is if there is a way of linking the exhibits so that is known that they are related; if it's not possible, it's not possible. The other point that you had raised, Mr. Whiting, was the question of statements being given in hard copy if they are -- if we know we are going to use them. Mr. Milovancevic, do you have anything to say to that? Do you think you can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. If that is easier, and it seems to be easier and more efficient, so we agree. No problem there. All we need to know is that that's what it's going to be like for the future. But I wanted to say something else in respect of what Mr. Whiting has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are rather worried about the situation today, that is to say that we don't have another witness, whereas yesterday we had to work overtime with a completely different schedule and to adapt our cross-examination to those extraordinary circumstances, only to be told today that the Prosecutor thought that Mr. Kirudja would be cross-examined today as well. All I can do now is ask them what this is all about. Why would the Defence team be placed in this position for us to adjourn early because there's no other witness for today? I don't think that is serious behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any answer, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I thought I had explained it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought so, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But what happened was -- I'm losing track of my days. But yesterday, yesterday we were looking at the schedule and it seemed quite clear to us that Mr. Kirudja would continue into today and then we would have this witness and it would basically fill today, and we would not have the need for another witness. So in the morning the first thing we did was we arranged for the witness, the expert, Mr. Poje, to go back, particularly since we did not want him to sit for three days in The Hague in the interruption of his testimony. Subsequent -- after we had made those arrangements, we learned this information about Mr. Kirudja, that he needed to get back, if possible, today and so we -- in the morning. And so then we took the steps to see if we could have a longer sitting, which was not resolved until shortly before the -- we sat and it wasn't -- even when we had taken those steps, it was not clear that we would finish with him yesterday. So we did not then go back and bring Mr. Poje back. It had already been done. He was already on his way to the airport, so it could not be changed. So -- and then finally I don't think -- I would note that Mr. Milovancevic finished with plenty of time yesterday, his cross-examination, and I think it was made clear to him that if he needed to go into today to continue his cross that would be possible. So I don't think he can claim any prejudice here from anything that has occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it my understanding -- correct understanding that in fact the arrangement to sit a little out of kilter with our normal arrangement yesterday was primarily to accommodate Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was completely to accommodate Mr. Kirudja. That was the only reason to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was the only reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So today there was nothing -- there was nobody to accommodate?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Even if you had a witness for today you would still have asked for what you asked for yesterday, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Sorry, Judge Nosworthy was just reminding me to say, the registrar, as you assign those exhibit numbers you will do that out of court. You don't have to bother to try and do them now. Thank you so much. Anyway, Mr. Milovancevic, you say you will try to accommodate that request that we have hard copies of statements if we think we are going to -- if we know we are going to use them in cross-examination or in examination-in-chief. Thank you so much for that. I guess you heard the answer from Mr. Whiting. I don't think I want to take the matter any further. The only comment I would like to make is on the request for hard copy statements, that when we do an assessment of the e-court we shall then say it is so inefficient we need the hard copies of statements. Court is going to adjourn now. We will reconvene on Tuesday, the 6th of June at 9.00 in the morning in this courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
